messages.subject: Dealing with multiple hierarchies
parts:
Hello hbayesdm-users,

I’m hoping to apply the ug_delta model to estimate individual learning rates from an ultimatum game. However, there are two groups of participants (older vs younger adults), and each participant experiences three different conditions while playing the game. In the end I would like to estimate one learning rate for each participant during each condition. If I understand correctly, the documentation suggests that to compare different groups I should be fitting separate models for each group (https://ccs-lab.github.io/hBayesDM/articles/getting_started.html#compare-models-and-groups), but I was unsure of the best way to handle the conditions within groups. Should I fit three models, one for each condition, and just pull out the individual parameters? Or should I fit six different models, one for each group*condition? Or just one model but give each subject*condition a unique identifier?

Each of these methods ignores some of the hierarchical information but I wanted to be extra careful that the parameters don’t get biased by ignoring some of this information. We ultimately want to answer the question of whether there is a group*condition interaction in learning rate (i.e., norm adaptation). So, our plan was to take the individual estimates and feed them into a 2x3 ANOVA.

Thanks for any advice!

Jeff

parts:
Hey just following up here.
I ended up running this model 2 ways. Once where the data was separated out for each condition (in this case partner) and one where I added a suffix based on the partner to the participant_id. For most parameters the outcome is pretty similar, however, for one of the parameters of interest, epsilon, there is a real divergence between the values I get. I've attached a scatterplot of the individual parameters. Each point is a parameter value for a particular participant for a particular partner. Along the x-axis is the value based on the model where the data was separated, along the y-axis when I just added a suffix to the participant ID.

messages.author: 4bcf82a01cf98f56
messages.subject: Re: Dealing with multiple hierarchies
parts:
Hi Jeff,

Many apologies for the long delay!

I believe the best way is to use three different learning rates for each condition as a within-subject design and fit each group separately. Please check this post for a within-subject modeling: https://groups.google.com/g/hbayesdm-users/c/E0m7Y90HWnw
"a group*condition interaction in learning rate (i.e., norm adaptation). So, our plan was to take the individual estimates and feed them into a 2x3 ANOVA."

--> I'm not sure how you can examine a group * condition interaction though. And I don't think you can feed them into a conventional 2x3 ANOVA with parameters estimated with such a hierarchical approach. For example, please check out this paper. 


Boehm, U., Marsman, M., Matzke, D., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2018). On the importance of avoiding shortcuts in applying cognitive models to hierarchical data. Behavior Research Methods, 50(4), 1614–1631. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1054-3

 

Best,
Young
